nodes.name: Alabama white sauce wings
nodes.blurb: Wings smoked over hickory and then coated or dunked in white sauce — a mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce with vinegar, lemon juice, black pepper, salt, and in many versions cayenne and horseradish.

nodes.name: Lemon pepper wings
nodes.blurb: A wing cooked without breading and finished in lemon pepper — granulated lemon zest mashed with cracked black pepper, then baked and dried, usually with salt and sugar in the blend. Atlanta orders it two ways.

nodes.name: Old Bay wings
nodes.blurb: A wing finished in Old Bay — a blend of eighteen herbs and spices built in Baltimore in 1939, celery salt first, with red and black pepper and paprika, and bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger among the…

nodes.name: Buffalo wings
nodes.blurb: A chicken wing cut into a drumette and a flat, deep-fried bare — no batter, no flour — then shaken in a bowl with melted butter and a vinegar-based cayenne pepper sauce, and served hot with celery, carrot sticks and a…

nodes.name: Jerk wings
nodes.blurb: Wings dry-rubbed or wet-marinated in Jamaican jerk seasoning and cooked over fire until the outside blackens.

nodes.name: Chicago mild sauce wings
nodes.blurb: Wings fried hard — left in the oil past golden until the skin goes dark and brittle — then handed over a counter in a box with french fries and a slice of white bread, the whole box doused in mild sauce.

nodes.name: Mumbo sauce wings
nodes.blurb: Fried chicken wings, usually whole and uncut, sold through the window of a Washington carryout and drowned in mumbo sauce — red, sweeter than barbecue sauce and by turns sharper or more sour, depending whose kitchen…

nodes.name: Garlic parmesan wings
nodes.blurb: A fried wing tossed in melted butter or oil with garlic and grated parmesan, often with dried herbs and black pepper, sometimes finished with more cheese out of the bowl so it sits in visible flecks.

nodes.name: Korean fried chicken wings
nodes.blurb: Chicken fried twice so the crust comes out thin and brittle — Julia Moskin of The New York Times called it "thin, crackly and almost transparent" — then hand-painted with sauce by brush rather than shaken in a bowl, so…

nodes.name: Memphis dry-rub wings
nodes.blurb: A wing finished with the rub that Memphis puts on ribs — salt and a spice blend, house by house, usually paprika-led — and handed over without sauce.

nodes.name: Nashville hot wings
nodes.blurb: Hot chicken's method put on a wing: marinate in a water- or buttermilk-based seasoned blend, flour, fry, then paint with a cayenne paste loosened with fat drawn from the fryer.

nodes.name: Rochester breaded wings
nodes.blurb: A chicken wing dredged in seasoned flour before it goes in the oil, fried until the coating sets hard, then glazed rather than tossed loose — most often in Country Sweet, a sweet-and-tangy sauce a Rochester kitchen…

nodes.name: Smoked barbecue wings
nodes.blurb: A wing cooked on a barbecue pit rather than in oil: rubbed, smoked over wood until the fat renders, then finished — brushed with a tomato sauce and set over higher heat to tack up, or dropped briefly in the fryer so the…

nodes.name: Alabama white sauce
nodes.blurb: A mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce, thin, pale and sharp. Typical ingredients are vinegar, lemon juice, salt, pepper, cayenne pepper and horseradish stirred into mayonnaise.

nodes.name: Blue cheese dressing
nodes.blurb: A thick white dip of blue cheese with mayonnaise and buttermilk, sour cream or yogurt, plus milk, vinegar, onion powder and garlic powder.

nodes.name: Buffalo sauce
nodes.blurb: Cayenne pepper hot sauce cut with melted butter. Two things, warmed together and held warm, poured over fried wings in a metal bowl and shaken.

nodes.name: Crystal Hot Sauce
nodes.blurb: A reddish-orange Louisiana pepper sauce made by Baumer Foods since 1923: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar, salt. Three ingredients on the 6 fl oz bottle; the gallon jug adds xanthan gum.

nodes.name: Frank's RedHot
aliases: Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce
nodes.blurb: A thin orange cayenne pepper sauce: aged cayenne red peppers, distilled vinegar, water, salt, garlic powder, in that order on the label. McCormick & Company makes it.

nodes.name: Garlic parmesan sauce
nodes.blurb: A pale, garlicky wing coating with parmesan in it. Two versions share the name: a creamy emulsified sauce built on oil and egg yolk with parmesan powder, sold bottled; and a kitchen mix of melted butter, minced garlic…

nodes.name: Honey barbecue sauce
nodes.blurb: A thick sweet red sauce: corn syrup or sugar, vinegar, tomato, honey, smoke flavour and spices. Sticky enough to hold on a wing without butter, sweet enough to caramelise under a broiler or on a grill.

nodes.name: Hot honey
nodes.blurb: Honey with chillies in it. Sweet first, then a heat that builds slowly — the flavour writers describe as "sweet-first" with a "slow-building heat".

nodes.name: Jerk marinade
nodes.blurb: A wet marinade, or a dry rub, built on allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers — both native to Jamaica and grown there by the Taíno.

nodes.name: Lemon pepper
nodes.blurb: A dry blend of granulated lemon zest and cracked black peppercorns. The zest is mashed into the pepper so citrus oil soaks in, then the mix is baked and dried.

nodes.name: Lemon pepper wet
nodes.blurb: A wing that has been through something wet and then through lemon pepper.

nodes.name: Mango habanero
nodes.blurb: A sweet-then-hot wing sauce: mango purée and corn syrup in front, habanero and cayenne behind. Orange, thick, and built to be tossed.

nodes.name: Memphis dry rub
nodes.blurb: A dry mix of salt, paprika, sugar and spices, patted onto meat before it cooks and shaken over it again after.

nodes.name: Mild sauce
nodes.blurb: A red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and wings on Chicago's South and West Sides. Recipes vary a great deal; many versions combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce.

nodes.name: Mumbo sauce
nodes.blurb: A carryout condiment of Washington, D.C.: red-orange, thick, poured over fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice.

nodes.name: Nashville hot paste
nodes.blurb: A cayenne paste, spooned onto fried chicken the moment it leaves the fryer.

nodes.name: Old Bay Seasoning
nodes.blurb: A blend of eighteen herbs and spices built on celery salt — salt and celery seed — with red pepper, black pepper and paprika.

nodes.name: Ranch dressing
nodes.blurb: A savoury creamy dressing of buttermilk, salt, garlic, onion, black pepper and herbs — commonly chives, parsley and dill — mixed into mayonnaise or another oil emulsion.

nodes.name: Soy garlic sauce
nodes.blurb: A brown glaze of soy sauce, sugar and garlic, brushed onto fried chicken after the fryer. Sweet and savoury rather than hot; often heavily garlicky.

nodes.name: Sweet chili sauce
aliases: น้ำจิ้มไก่
nodes.blurb: A clear, thickened red sauce of chillies, rice wine vinegar and sugar, often with garlic and sometimes fish sauce. Red chilli peppers — Fresno, Thai or red jalapeños — give it its flecks.

nodes.name: Teriyaki sauce
nodes.blurb: Soy sauce, mirin or sake, and sugar, boiled down to a glaze. The Japanese name for it is tare (タレ).

nodes.name: Yangnyeom sauce
nodes.blurb: A sweet and spicy glaze built on gochujang — a fermented Korean paste of red chili powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean powder, barley malt powder and salt — with garlic, sugar and other seasonings.

nodes.name: beef on weck
nodes.blurb: Rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, on a kummelweck roll topped with kosher salt and caraway seeds.

nodes.name: boneless wings
nodes.blurb: Small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget, and tossed in or served with the same sauces as a Buffalo wing.

nodes.name: buffalo chicken dip
nodes.blurb: Shredded chicken, cream cheese, cayenne-and-butter wing sauce and a dairy dressing, baked until it bubbles and eaten hot with chips, celery or bread.

nodes.name: buffalo chicken pizza
nodes.blurb: A pizza sauced with cayenne-and-butter wing sauce instead of tomato, topped with chicken and mozzarella, and finished with blue cheese or ranch.

nodes.name: celery and carrots
nodes.blurb: Cut celery, usually with carrot sticks, served cold beside hot wings with a cup of blue cheese or ranch that both the vegetables and the wings go into.

nodes.name: chicken and waffles
nodes.blurb: Fried chicken on a waffle, eaten with butter and syrup as a waffle would be, and often with hot sauce.

nodes.name: chicken riggies
nodes.blurb: An Italian-American pasta dish from the Utica–Rome area of New York: chicken, rigatoni, and hot or sweet peppers in a spicy cream-and-tomato sauce. Variations are many; the peppers and the rigatoni are the constants.

nodes.name: french fries
nodes.blurb: Potatoes cut into even batonnet or julienne strips, dried, and deep-fried.

nodes.name: the fried rice plate
nodes.blurb: Whole fried chicken wings served over egg fried rice with mumbo sauce, sold from Chinese-American carryouts across the Washington, D.C. metropolitan region.

nodes.name: Garbage Plate
nodes.blurb: Hot dog or hamburger meat and a meat hot sauce piled on a bed of side dishes — usually macaroni salad and home fries — with onions and mustard, and buttered bread alongside.

nodes.name: jojo potatoes
nodes.blurb: A potato wedge that has been breaded, pressure-fried and spiced — not a bare wedge, and not a fry. The pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so the potato cooks fast and hard while keeping its water.

nodes.name: mozzarella sticks
nodes.blurb: Elongated pieces of mozzarella coated in breadcrumbs or batter and fried, served as an hors d'oeuvre with marinara. On a wing menu they are the thing a table orders when half of it does not want wings.

nodes.name: mumbo fries
nodes.blurb: French fries under mumbo sauce, from a Washington, D.C. carryout.

nodes.name: pickled radish
nodes.blurb: Cubed pickled daikon in a sweet-sour brine, served cold in a small tub beside Korean fried chicken.

nodes.name: pizza logs
nodes.blurb: Mozzarella, and often pepperoni, rolled in an egg-roll wrapper and deep-fried, served with marinara to dip.

nodes.name: the pitcher
nodes.blurb: Draught beer sold by the jug for a table to share. It is the other half of a wing order almost everywhere wings are sold, and in two traditions it is named into the food: Hooters built its concept on wings and beer, and…

nodes.name: white bread and pickles
nodes.blurb: Two slices of plain white sandwich bread with pickle chips on top, and the hot chicken laid over both. The bread catches the cayenne paste and the fat coming off the bird; the pickles cut it.

nodes.name: the wing basket
nodes.blurb: The unit a bar sells wings in: a count of pieces in a basket or on a plate, lined with paper, with celery and carrots, a cup of blue cheese or ranch, and usually fries.

nodes.name: the air fryer
nodes.blurb: A small countertop convection oven that reaches deep-frying temperatures without submerging the food in oil.

nodes.name: the baking powder bake
nodes.blurb: The home method that gets wing skin to crisp in an oven: toss dried wings with baking powder and salt, bake low to render and dry, then hot to brown.

nodes.name: the breaded fry
nodes.blurb: Coating a wing before it goes in the oil — flour, seasoned flour, batter or crumbs — so the crust rather than the skin carries the crunch and holds the sauce.

nodes.name: the brine
nodes.blurb: Salting the bird before it cooks. Brining treats food with brine or coarse salt, which preserves and seasons it while enhancing tenderness.

nodes.name: the deep fryer
nodes.blurb: The machine or pot the wing goes into: food submerged in hot fat rather than shallow-fried in a pan. A commercial vat, a chip pan, a wok, a Dutch oven or a cast-iron pot all do it.

nodes.name: the double fry
nodes.blurb: Frying in two passes with a rest between them. The first pass cooks the piece through and drives water out of the skin; the rest lets the surface dry and the interior even out; the second pass, hotter, builds the crust.

nodes.name: the dredge
nodes.blurb: Coating food before it fries. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food — cornmeal, flour or tempura — and breadcrumbs may be used.

nodes.name: frying oil
nodes.blurb: What the wing is cooked in. Deep frying submerges food in hot fat — traditionally lard, today most commonly oil — and the choice of fat sets flavour, how long the vat lasts, what the shop pays and what goes on the…

nodes.name: the grill
nodes.blurb: Cooking the wing over direct heat instead of in oil. Buffalo's own reference text lists it among the alternatives — traditionally deep-fried, but alternatively baked, grilled, or broiled — and the Anchor Bar's account…

nodes.name: the naked fry
nodes.blurb: Frying a wing with nothing on it — no batter, no flour, no crumb. The skin browns and crisps on its own, the fat under it renders into the oil, and the sauce goes on afterwards.

nodes.name: the par-cook
nodes.blurb: Cooking the wing most of the way in advance and finishing it to order. The first pass drives out water and cooks the meat through; the finishing pass, hotter and short, browns it.

nodes.name: sauce on the side
nodes.blurb: Ordering the wings unsauced with the sauce in a cup. The argument is whether the sauce is a step in the cooking or a condiment at the table — and the traditions answer it differently, on the record, in their own methods.

nodes.name: smoke then fry
nodes.blurb: Cooking the wing through in smoke, then dropping it briefly into hot oil or onto high heat to tighten the skin. Smoke gives flavour and colour that a fryer cannot; the fryer gives a crust that smoke alone leaves flabby.

nodes.name: the toss
nodes.blurb: The metal bowl. Cooked wings go into a bowl or pot, sauce goes over them, and the whole thing is shaken to coat the wings completely before serving.

nodes.name: the wing cut
nodes.blurb: Where the knife goes on a chicken wing. The wing comes off the bird in three segments and the cook cuts it at both joints: the drumette, shaped like a small drumstick and white meat; the middle flat, also called the…

nodes.name: American Deli
nodes.blurb: A counter chain out of Atlanta, open since 1989, that sells wings by the ten-piece with a long board of seasonings and sauces.

nodes.name: Anchor Bar
nodes.blurb: A bar and restaurant at Main and North in Buffalo, open since 1935, which claims the Buffalo wing and has trademarked the phrase. Frank and Teressa Bellissimo opened it; their son Dominic ran it and sold the story.

nodes.name: Atomic Wings
nodes.blurb: A New York wing chain founded in 1989 by a man trying to reproduce what he had eaten as a student in Buffalo.

nodes.name: Bar-Bill Tavern
nodes.blurb: A tavern on Main Street in East Aurora, fifteen miles southeast of Buffalo and not in the city at all, whose wings are brushed with sauce by hand rather than tossed.

nodes.name: Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q
nodes.blurb: The Decatur, Alabama pit where white barbecue sauce was invented: mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper, made for smoked chicken.

nodes.name: Blondies Sports
nodes.blurb: A sports bar on West 79th Street between Amsterdam and Broadway, on Manhattan's Upper West Side, with televisions in every sightline and a wing order most of the room is there for.

nodes.name: Bolton's Spicy Chicken & Fish
nodes.blurb: A small East Nashville counter at 624 Main Street selling spicy fried chicken and spicy fried fish, opened in 1997 by Bolton Matthews and Dolly Ingram. The recipe came down from Matthews's uncle Bolton Polk.

nodes.name: Bonchon
nodes.blurb: A Korean fried chicken chain that fries each piece twice and paints the sauce on with a brush.

nodes.name: Buffalo Wild Wings
nodes.blurb: A sports-bar chain that put a Buffalo wing on a menu in Columbus, Ohio in 1982 and then on menus in all fifty states.

nodes.name: Capital City Mambo Sauce
nodes.blurb: A bottler, not a counter. Arsha and Charles Jones started Capital City in a home kitchen in 2011 to put D.C.

nodes.name: Central BBQ
nodes.blurb: A Memphis barbecue house started in 2002 by two competition cooks, Craig Blondis and Roger Sapp, on Central Avenue.

nodes.name: Chickie's & Pete's
nodes.blurb: A Philadelphia sports bar and crab house that began as a Mayfair taproom in 1977 and now runs stadium, casino and airport rooms.

nodes.name: Ching's Hot Wings
nodes.blurb: A Memphis wing shop on Getwell Road, trading since 2003, selling whole wings by the piece from three to four hundred.

nodes.name: Country Sweet Chicken & Ribs
nodes.blurb: A Rochester counter open since 1977, hand-breading its wings and glazing them in a sauce the founder built in a home kitchen and the city now buys by the bottle.

nodes.name: Duff's Famous Wings
nodes.blurb: A wing house at Sheridan Drive and Millersport Highway in Amherst, north of Buffalo, open under that corner since 1946 and selling wings since 1969.

nodes.name: Elmo's Bar & Restaurant
nodes.blurb: A pitcher-and-television sports bar on Millersport Highway in Getzville, near the University at Buffalo's north campus, whose signature is a wing that goes through the fryer and then onto a grill.

nodes.name: Gabriel's Gate
nodes.blurb: A restaurant and tavern at 145 Allen Street in Buffalo's Allentown, trading since 1969 inside an 1864 brick row house with tin ceilings and two wood-burning fireplaces.

nodes.name: Harold's Chicken Shack
nodes.blurb: A Chicago fried-chicken institution founded by Harold Pierce in 1950 and franchised to friends and family, now past a hundred storefronts.

nodes.name: Hattie B's Hot Chicken
nodes.blurb: A Nashville hot chicken house founded by a father and son both named Nick Bishop, open in Midtown since 2012 and now in seven cities.

nodes.name: Hooters
nodes.blurb: A restaurant chain that sells breaded wings, beer and a uniform. Six Clearwater, Florida businessmen incorporated Hooters, Inc.

nodes.name: Horace & Dickie's Seafood
nodes.blurb: A fried-fish carryout that ran thirty years at 12th and H Streets NE in Washington and now trades from Prince George's County, Maryland.

nodes.name: Jeremiah's Tavern
nodes.blurb: A tavern at 1104 Monroe Avenue in Rochester, the first of four rooms, frying wings that arrive "fresh, never frozen" in sauces the company mixes daily at its own commissary.

nodes.name: J.R. Crickets
nodes.blurb: A Midtown Atlanta wing bar open since 1982, founded by Paul Juliano, who still runs it.

nodes.name: La Nova Pizzeria
nodes.blurb: A pizzeria on West Ferry Street in Buffalo's west side, run by three generations of the Todaro family, whose barbecue wing is the local counter-argument to cayenne and butter.

nodes.name: Mammoser's Tavern & Restaurant
nodes.blurb: A neighbourhood tavern on South Buffalo Street in Hamburg, twelve miles south of the city, pouring eighteen microbrew drafts and frying a wing in a house sauce built on four kinds of pepper.

nodes.name: Nine-Eleven Tavern
nodes.blurb: A cash-only corner tavern in South Buffalo, established 1981, whose wings come out large and heavily sauced in a recipe its late owner kept to himself.

nodes.name: Peppa's Jerk Chicken
nodes.blurb: A Jamaican takeout counter on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn's Little Caribbean, run by Gavin Hussey, whose jerk chicken is dry-rubbed, washed with vinegar and charred black before it is hacked apart to order.

nodes.name: Prince's Hot Chicken Shack
nodes.blurb: The Nashville hot chicken shack, started by James Thornton Prince and run since 1980 by his great-niece André Prince Jeffries.

nodes.name: Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken
nodes.blurb: A West Side Chicago fried-chicken counter whose sauce is in its name. Gus W. Rickette Sr. and Mary F.

nodes.name: The Wing Cafe & Tap House
aliases: The Wing Cafe and Tap House
nodes.blurb: A wing bar on Roswell Road in east Cobb County, outside Atlanta, carrying thirty-five to forty sauces and marinades and thirty to fifty beers on tap.

nodes.name: Wingnutz
nodes.blurb: A sports bar on Millersport Highway in Williamsville, run by Ed and Alicia Wrazen, whose wings ran for thirteen years out of a Knights of Columbus hall before they had a restaurant.

nodes.name: Wingstop
nodes.blurb: A fast-food chain built on one part of the bird. Antonio Swad and Bernadette Fiaschetti opened the first Wingstop in Garland, Texas in 1994 and franchised it from 1997; the company is headquartered in Dallas and counted…

nodes.name: Yum's II Carry-Out
nodes.blurb: A Chinese carryout on 14th Street NW in Washington, open past two most nights, selling fried wings, fried rice and french fries with mumbo sauce over them. It is the first address on most D.C. carryout lists.

nodes.name: Adrian Miller
nodes.blurb: Food writer and historian of African American cooking, based in Denver.

nodes.name: Al Morganti
nodes.blurb: Philadelphia hockey writer and broadcaster, born 28 May 1953, and the man Wing Bowl is credited to.

nodes.name: André Prince Jeffries
nodes.blurb: Took over her great-uncle Thornton Prince's café in 1980, dropped the BBQ out of its name, and has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since.

nodes.name: Angelo Cataldi
nodes.blurb: Philadelphia sports-radio morning host, born 13 March 1951, whose WIP show founded Wing Bowl in 1993 and ran it for twenty-six years.

nodes.name: Antonio Swad
nodes.blurb: Founded Wingstop in Garland, Texas in 1994 with Bernadette Fiaschetti, franchised it from 1997, and sold it in 2003 at ninety units. He had already built Pizza Patrón, started 1986, and sold that in 2017.

nodes.name: Argia B. Collins
nodes.blurb: Chicago barbecue man who made and bottled Mumbo sauce, and whose trademark on the name later beat a Washington, D.C. company that had been selling a sauce called mumbo for years.

nodes.name: Bill "El Wingador" Simmons
nodes.blurb: Five-time Wing Bowl champion, born 1 November 1961, and the contest's own house name — El Wingador, 6 foot 5 and 290 pounds at his peak.

nodes.name: Bob Gibson
nodes.blurb: Decatur, Alabama barbecue man, 1888 to 1972, who dunked hickory-smoked chicken in a sauce of mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper.

nodes.name: Calvin Trillin
nodes.blurb: American journalist and food writer, born 5 December 1935 in Kansas City, Missouri. He joined The New Yorker in 1963 and wrote its "U.S. Journal" series from 1967 to 1982, a piece a month from somewhere in the country.

nodes.name: Dominic Bellissimo
nodes.blurb: Son of Frank and Teressa Bellissimo, tending the Anchor Bar on the night the house dates its wings to, 4 March 1964. He later owned the bar and spent decades promoting it and the wing. He died in March 1991, aged 68.

nodes.name: Drew Cerza
nodes.blurb: Founded the National Buffalo Wing Festival in 2002 and runs it. A marketing man by trade, he took the idea from a film that invented a Buffalo wing festival that did not exist, and built the one that does.

nodes.name: Frank Bellissimo
nodes.blurb: Opened the Anchor Bar in Buffalo with his wife Teressa in 1935 and ran the front of the house. His account of the first wings turns on a delivery that went wrong.

nodes.name: Harold Pierce
nodes.blurb: Founded Harold's Chicken Shack in Chicago on 22 June 1950 and built it into the South Side's fried chicken chain, where a wing dinner comes cut over fries and drowned in mild sauce.

nodes.name: Jim Disbrow
nodes.blurb: Figure skater, skating official and co-founder of Buffalo Wild Wings, born 9 July 1948 and dead of brain cancer on 16 October 2002, aged 54.

nodes.name: Joey Chestnut
nodes.blurb: American competitive eater, born 25 November 1983 in Fulton County, Kentucky and raised in Vallejo, California.

nodes.name: John Young
nodes.blurb: Sold chicken wings whole and uncut — breaded, deep-fried, and coated in a tomato-based sauce he called mumbo, or mambo — from a restaurant on Buffalo's East Side in the 1960s.

nodes.name: Teressa Bellissimo
nodes.blurb: Cooked at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, which she opened with her husband Frank in 1935 and lived above.

nodes.name: Thornton Prince
nodes.blurb: Nashville cook whose family café put cayenne paste on fried chicken and made a city's dish out of it.

nodes.name: Buffalo Wing Trail
nodes.blurb: A list of wing joints, published by Visit Buffalo Niagara, the region's tourism bureau.

nodes.name: City of Buffalo
nodes.blurb: The municipal government that put its name on the wing, and then put a day on the calendar. Buffalo was incorporated as a city in 1832, seven years after the Erie Canal chose it for a terminus.

nodes.name: National Chicken Council
nodes.blurb: The trade association of the US chicken industry, and the keeper of the number every Super Bowl story quotes.

nodes.name: Southern Foodways Alliance
nodes.blurb: An archive that records what cooks say about their own work. The Southern Foodways Alliance is based at the University of Mississippi's Center for the Study of Southern Culture and, in its own words, "documents…

nodes.name: U.S. Poultry & Egg Association
nodes.blurb: The trade association that funds the research and runs the equipment show behind the bird.

nodes.name: National Buffalo Wing Festival
nodes.blurb: A two-day wing festival held on Labor Day weekend at Sahlen Field, the minor-league ballpark in downtown Buffalo. Drew Cerza founded it in 2002.

nodes.name: National Chicken Wing Day
nodes.blurb: A food day on 29 July, kept by bars, chains and marketing departments across the United States.

nodes.name: Super Bowl Sunday

facets.when: the second Sunday in February, since 2022

nodes.blurb: The biggest wing day in the United States, and the second-biggest American eating day of any kind after Thanksgiving dinner.

nodes.name: Wing Bowl

facets.when: the Friday before the Super Bowl

nodes.blurb: A competitive wing-eating contest run by a Philadelphia sports radio station on the Friday before the Super Bowl.

nodes.name: all flats
nodes.blurb: An order that refuses half the bird. A wing splits one-for-one into a drumette and a flat, so a kitchen filling an all-flats order has to sell the drumettes to somebody else — which is why the answer is often no, and…

nodes.name: atomic
nodes.blurb: Top of a house heat ladder, and a word that only means something inside one bar's list. Wingstop's own description of its Atomic flavour is "It's the hottest we've got.

nodes.name: boneless
nodes.blurb: Breast meat cut into pieces, floured and spiced, fried or baked, then sauced like a wing and sold under the wing's name.

nodes.name: Buffalo
nodes.blurb: A city's name working as an adjective. Buffalo now modifies a sauce rather than a place: vinegar-based cayenne hot sauce cut with melted butter, and anything wearing it.

nodes.name: drumette
nodes.blurb: Upper of the three wing segments, and the meatiest. One bone, meat bunched at one end, skin all round: it eats like a small drumstick, which is where the name comes from. White meat, same as the breast. Two per bird.

nodes.name: extra crispy
nodes.blurb: An order for more time in the oil. Not a flavour, not an upcharge in most places: a request that the wing stay down until the skin goes hard and the colour goes past golden.

nodes.name: flapper
nodes.blurb: Cook's name for the wing tip: the pointed third segment, the one that carried the flight feathers. Skin and cartilage over two thin bones.

nodes.name: flat
nodes.blurb: Middle segment, two bones with a gap between them, and more skin per bite than any other piece of a chicken. Flat because it is — it lies down in the fryer basket and comes out on one plane. Two per bird.

nodes.name: hot honey
nodes.blurb: Honey infused with chillies, and the two-word name that turned it into a menu category. On wings it is a finish rather than a toss: drizzled over crust after the sauce, or whisked into a sauce to sweeten and thicken it.

nodes.name: mild sauce
nodes.blurb: Chicago's word for a red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and fries at South and West Side chicken shacks and barbecue counters, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago.

nodes.name: mumbo
nodes.blurb: A word for a sweet-sour-hot red condiment, sold behind plexiglass in Washington carryouts and poured on fried wings, french fries, jumbo shrimp and fried rice.

nodes.name: naked
nodes.blurb: Unbreaded. A wing fried in nothing but its own skin, no flour, no batter, no dredge. Hooters, which breads by hand as its original style, lists the alternative as Naked Wings and describes them: "Traditional style.

nodes.name: party wing
nodes.blurb: A supermarket's name for wings already broken down: tips off, joint cut, drumettes and flats loose in one bag or tray. The work a bar's prep cook does, done at the plant.

nodes.name: weck
nodes.blurb: Half of a sandwich name that lost its other half. Weck is the kummelweck roll: kosher salt and caraway seeds baked onto the top, softer and fluffier than the German Kümmelbrötchen it descends from.

nodes.name: wet and dry
nodes.blurb: A two-way choice about the finish, asked after you have picked a flavour. Dry means the cooked wing gets tossed in seasoning — powder on crust.

nodes.name: wing night
nodes.blurb: A weekly price special on wings, usually sold by the piece and usually paired with a drink minimum. The deal is the draw; the pitcher is the margin.

nodes.name: wing tip
nodes.blurb: Third segment, the pointed end. Skin, cartilage, two slivers of bone, almost no meat.

nodes.name: wing
nodes.blurb: A chicken's wing, and the pieces it becomes. Off the bird it runs drumette, flat and tip; a kitchen cuts it at both joints and usually throws the tip into stock, so what a menu calls a wing is one of two pieces.

nodes.name: Buffalo murals
nodes.blurb: Buffalo paints its own story on its walls, and the wing is part of what gets painted.

nodes.name: Chicken shack signs
nodes.blurb: The sign over a wing or fried-chicken counter is a working document. It has to be readable from a car at thirty miles an hour, name the shop, say CHICKEN, and usually price something.

nodes.name: Hot sauce labels
nodes.blurb: A hot sauce label sells one thing before it sells any other: how much it will hurt.

nodes.name: Neon chicken
nodes.blurb: A chicken drawn in bent glass tube, filled with gas, and run off a transformer over a bar, a drive-in or a wing counter.

nodes.name: Rooster weathervanes
nodes.blurb: A rooster cut or moulded in sheet metal, balanced on a spindle, and put on a roof to show which way the wind blows.

nodes.name: Wing festival posters
nodes.blurb: A wing festival poster does four things at once: names the event, fixes the date and the gate, lists the sponsors in descending size, and supplies a mascot the event can print on a T-shirt.

nodes.name: Boneless is not a wing
nodes.blurb: On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio held, 4 to 3, that a diner who swallowed a chicken bone from a boneless wing could not take his negligence claim to a jury, because he could reasonably have guarded against it.

nodes.name: Free to use
nodes.blurb: Every map, price, coordinate and recipe on this site comes from somewhere a reader can go and check.

nodes.name: Ranch against blue cheese
nodes.blurb: Buffalo sends out blue cheese. America buys ranch. Blue cheese reached the wing plate on the first night of the Anchor Bar story, off the antipasto tray, and it is still the house cup along the city's wing trail.

nodes.name: The flat and the drum
nodes.blurb: A chicken wing has three joints and yields two pieces a kitchen will sell: the drumette, which is the humerus with the meat pushed to one end, and the flat, which is the two-boned middle section carrying most of the…

nodes.name: The origin fight
nodes.blurb: Two Buffalo kitchens claim the wing, and neither claim rests on a document. The Anchor Bar dates the dish to the night of 4 March 1964 and tells the story three different ways.

nodes.name: The price of a wing
nodes.blurb: In 1964 the wing was the cheapest thing on the bird, which is the premise every origin story rests on.
